| # | Cost | Godot | macOS | Gap | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Directional shadows (two suns): maps + sampling | 7.4 ms GPU/frame at 1080p (maps 3.1 incl. the atlas clear; sampling makes the opaque and transparent passes 5.0 ms slower, partly overlapping); maps 3.1 ms at 540p | ~1.4 ms at 1080p (two maps 1.8 ms; turning shadows off saves 1.4 ms) | **~6 ms at 1080p** | `--benchmark-no-shadows`: 22.1 -> 14.7 ms, 29 -> 45 FPS. Godot's soft filter alone (SoftHigh vs hard, `REDACTED`) is 3.7 ms. Godot renders four maps (two suns x two splits) into an 8192² atlas and clears the whole atlas every frame (0.34 ms); SceneKit renders one 4096 and one 2048 map. |
| 2 | Scene shading without shadows (opaque + transparent passes) | 9.1 ms at 1080p | 5.7 ms (one forward pass) | **~3.4 ms** | Fill-bound: the opaque pass scales 2.5x and the transparent pass 3x from 540p to 1080p. The opaque cost is the ground: without the town it is unchanged (7.6 ms), with the `townNoise` ground materials made constant it drops by 2.2 ms. The transparent pass is 15 draws of town ground overlays (soil, street, trampled sand, red soil) for 6.6 ms with shadows, 3.9 without; without the town 2.7. |
| 3 | Post-processing, depth prepass and frame overhead | ~4.1 ms (depth prepass 1.0, glow 1.0, tonemap + HUD 0.6, uploads 0.5, MSAA depth resolve 0.5, window blit 0.3, colour resolve 0.2) | ~0.6-1.0 ms (uploads 0.5, bloom and final blit; SceneKit has no depth prepass outside its SSAO pass) | **~3 ms** | Metal System Trace per encoder. |
| 4 | Loading freeze at 93 % (`startDirtTrack` on the main thread) | 2.8-3.4 s | 0.75 s | **2-2.6 s** | `--world-build-profile`: facade node flush 2.07 s + parallel mesh preparation 0.51 s for 4,884 nodes; `revealDirtTrack`'s `view.snapshot()` 0.47 s, of which PNG encoding of the discarded image 0.30 s; GC 0.12 s; game code ~0.2 s. SceneKit prepares in the background (`SCNView.prepare` is asynchronous there). |
| 5 | Main-thread CPU (one thread does everything) | 11 ms/frame at 540p: managed 4.1 ms (game tick 1.6, facade flush 2.1-2.5, ...), Godot's scene and render encoding 3.3 ms, Metal driver 1.5 ms; GC pauses ~1.2 ms/frame on average | main 3.8 ms + SceneKit render thread 8.4 ms (in parallel) | headroom 5.7 ms at 60 FPS | `sample` of both processes; the facade flush grows 2.1 -> 2.5 ms over ten minutes (trail chunks). |
| 6 | Garbage collection | 1.6 MB allocated per frame (tick 1.1 MB: effects 0.6, town 0.36; facade node flush 0.48 MB) -> 12-14 gen0 + ~1 gen1 per second, 16-19 ms paused per second | ARC, no collector | ~1 ms/frame, pauses of ~1.4 ms | `godot-render.json` allocation telemetry |
| 7 | Memory | 3.8-3.96 GB (editor) / 3.30-3.77 GB (export); .NET heap ~1 GB, textures 610 MB (540p) / 796 MB (1080p), buffers ~380 MB | 3.23 GB | +0.1-0.7 GB | process RSS, Godot monitors |
| 8 | Texture churn in the dunes | 49 new ImageTextures + 72 MTLTextures per second in `--dune-roam` (DeformableSand height maps, a new texture per patch update as on macOS); city roam: none after the first minute; race 1.3/s | (SceneKit creates the same MTLTextures) | small | `godot-render.json` `flushed` counters; freed only when the GC finalizes the wrappers |

## Method

**Same drawable, same conditions.** The macOS benchmark asks for a 960 x 540-point window (TownSmoke.swift: a 1080p
drawable on a Retina screen), which is a 960 x 540 drawable on this 1x display, and AppKit keeps titled windows inside
the visible frame, so not even a 1920 x 1080-point window fits. `tools/perf/window-inject.m`, loaded with
`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` (the macOS game is not modified; its ad-hoc signed binary allows it, as does the Godot editor
with `com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables`), turns that request into an exact 960 x 540 or
1920 x 1080-point window at the bottom left of the screen, at the floating window level. Godot runs at backing scale 1
(no `MARVIN_BACKING_SCALE`), so both games draw 1x HUDs over a drawable of exactly that size (confirmed by
`benchmark.json`'s `drawableWidth/Height` and the 1920 x 1080 `final-fps.png`). A black opaque backdrop window covers
the rest of the screen: a MarvinSimulator left running on this Mac presented 60 frames per second with 400-500
GPU-ms per second while visible; the macOS game's opaque 1080p window occluded it, Godot's window did not, which made the
first Godot run look worse than it was. With the backdrop it presents nothing in any run, but Metal System Trace still
shows it using 170-220 GPU-ms per second, and WindowServer 10-160, in every run of both games: absolute numbers are
pessimistic, the comparison is fair.

**Scenes.** `--town-benchmark` (TownSmoke.swift and its port: same flags, same 45 s, daylight 0.5) in its default race
mode (four racers on the track, chase camera with an overview every 24 s) and `--city-roam` (Marvin driving a fixed route
through the town). The race world is built during the launch in both (8.7 s from launch to the benchmark's start on
macOS, 12.7 s Godot editor runtime, 12.9 s export).

**What is recorded** (`tools/perf/run-benchmark.py`): the benchmark's own files (`benchmark.json`: rendered-frame
intervals; `timeline.json`: CPU time per tick phase); `metalperftrace listen` (Apple's always-on Metal statistics, no
HUD overhead): presented FPS, on-GPU walltime per frame, frame-on-glass intervals, and the other processes' GPU time;
process RSS and CPU per second; main-thread stalls (`main-stalls.m`, a run-loop timer in both apps); and for Godot
`godot-render.json` (per second: draw calls, nodes, objects, texture/buffer/heap memory, GC counts and pauses, CPU and
allocation per facade flush stage and per tick phase, textures created). **GPU per pass**: a 4 s Metal System Trace
(`xctrace`, 30 s after launch) with `metal-labels.m` loaded, which names every Metal encoder by its attachments
(format, size, MSAA, depth load/clear), draw count and compute pipelines. Godot's Metal driver sets no encoder labels
or debug groups and its RenderingDevice timestamps are zero on Metal, so neither Godot's visual profiler nor the trace's
default "Render Command N" names identify passes. `mst-gpu.py` sums each label's GPU intervals and the union of all of
a process's intervals (vertex, fragment and compute overlap on Apple GPUs). Two GPU numbers appear below:

The performance pass is past measurement and in the optimisation stage: three tracks running in parallel worktrees.

**Measured on this Mac** (a Mac mini M2, same scenes, same window sizes, one game at a time):

| | 960×540 | 1920×1080 |
|---|---|---|
| macOS game | 60 FPS | 60 FPS (11.0 ms graphics per frame) |
| Godot port | 59–60 FPS | 29 FPS town, 35 FPS race (22.1 ms graphics per frame) |

- **Not a C# problem:** the debug and release builds give the same frame rates.
- **Shadows:** about 6 ms of the 11 ms gap. Godot renders four shadow maps into one large shared map and clears all of it every frame; SceneKit renders two.
- **Ground surfaces:** about 3 ms. The noise-shaded town ground and its stacked transparent overlays are costly in Godot.
- **Post-processing:** about 3 ms. Godot does a depth pass, bloom and anti-aliasing resolves that SceneKit doesn't.
- **Loading:** Godot freezes 2.8–3.4 s at 93% (macOS: 0.75 s). Most of it is pushing 4,884 objects into the scene in one go, plus a 0.3 s screenshot that's thrown away.
- **Other findings:** no memory leak over 10 minutes for either game. Godot's garbage collector runs 12–14 times a second. The "2–15 fps transitions" from the earlier report were the test harness's own screenshots, not the game.

The full analysis is committed and pushed in `apps/simulator-godot/docs/performance.md`.

**Optimisation tracks:**
- **Graphics:** just started committing (measurement tooling so far).
- **CPU, loading and garbage collection:** no commits yet.
- **Release builds:** 7 commits so far:
  - macOS and Windows exports, with a layout check;
  - a Windows version of the `hypot` maths function that matches the Mac one bit for bit;
  - the remaining macOS-only code paths made portable;
  - keeping the window on screen on Windows;
  - a README on building and running on Windows.

Every track commit is backed up to a `godot-port/*` branch. When the tracks finish, an integration step replays each commit onto `codex/mos-aster-racing-city` with its own checkpoint and push. It then re-runs all the test modes and the comparison sheets, and re-measures.

Two of the three optimisation tracks are done. The graphics track, which is the one that matters for 1080p frame rate, is still running. Nothing is integrated into `codex/mos-aster-racing-city` yet; each track's commits are backed up on its `godot-port/*` branch.

**CPU, loading and memory track (done, 6 commits):**
- **Loading:** the freeze at 93% went from 2.8 s to 0.3 s, and launch to race from 15.0 s to 12.2 s.
- **Per-frame work:** the per-frame scene sync is about 40% cheaper, because it now only sends changed state to Godot. Memory allocated per frame fell from 1.6 MB to 0.6 MB, so garbage-collection pauses dropped from about 17 ms to 7 ms per second.
- **Textures:** new sand textures in the dunes fell from 49 per second to 1.7, because the rest are now updated in place.
- **Resets:** trail chunks, sand patches and floor details are now freed on reset. Over 10 minutes there's no growth beyond the trail marks, as on macOS.
- **Frame rate unchanged:** 60 FPS at 960×540 (vsync-capped) and about 29–34 FPS at 1080p (graphics-bound). These gains are headroom and smoothness.
- **Look unchanged:** the deterministic test reports are byte-identical, and captures are within run-to-run noise.

**Release builds track (done, 7 commits):**
- **Exports:** `tools/export [macos|windows]` builds both: a 528 MB macOS app and a 374 MB Windows folder (240 MB zipped).
- **Exported macOS app:** all test modes pass, plus the full scripted playthrough from menu to a three-lap race to the sandbox (63 of 63 steps). It also passes with Windows conventions switched on, at 150% scaling and on Vulkan.
- **Maths:** Windows gets a `hypot` that matches the Mac bit for bit. 600 million inputs were checked; .NET's own differs in 10% of game-range calls.
- **Windows still untested:** the build has never run on Windows. Untested there: Direct3D 12, audio output, the title bar and display scaling. Windows' `sin`, `cos`, `pow` and similar can also differ from the Mac in the last bit, so race results may drift slightly; the town layout should be unaffected because it uses a seeded generator.

**Graphics track (still running):** it has added GPU measurement tooling and one SSAO change so far. It's attacking the 22 ms vs 11 ms gap: shadows (about 6 ms of it), ground shading (about 3 ms) and post-processing (about 3 ms).

When it finishes, the integration step replays all three tracks onto `codex/mos-aster-racing-city` with a checkpoint and push per commit. It then re-runs every test mode and comparison sheet, and re-measures.

**Results.**
- **960x540:** both games hold 60 FPS, in the race and in the town roam, with 0–2 frames over 25 ms per 45 s run.
- **1920x1080:** macOS holds 60 FPS. Godot gets 29 FPS in the town roam and 35 FPS in the race, with 1,200–1,350 frames over 25 ms per 45 s run.
- **GPU work per frame:** Godot needs 22.1 ms against SceneKit's 11.0 ms at 1080p, and 9.7 ms against 7.9 ms at 540p. Even with the GPU to itself, Godot would top out at about 45 FPS at 1080p.

**Where the 11 ms gap at 1080p comes from** (Metal traces with every render pass named, plus runs with features switched off):
1. **Directional shadows, about 6 ms more.** Godot spends about 7.4 ms against SceneKit's 1.4 ms. It renders four shadow maps into an 8192² atlas, clears the whole atlas every frame, and its soft shadow filter alone costs 3.7 ms.
2. **Shading the ground, about 3.4 ms more.** Without shadows, Godot's opaque and transparent passes take 9.1 ms against SceneKit's 5.7 ms. The cost is the terrain plus the 15 transparent town ground overlays.
3. **Post-processing and the depth prepass, about 3 ms more.**
4. **SSAO costs the same in both games** (about 2 ms).

**CPU:** at 540p, Godot does everything on one main thread, which is 66% busy (11 ms of each 16.7 ms frame). SceneKit splits its work between a main thread (23% busy) and a render thread (50% busy). The game logic itself runs as fast as Swift's. Godot's main thread allocates 1.6 MB per frame, which triggers 12–14 small garbage collections per second, pausing the game 16–19 ms per second in total.

**Ten-minute town roam:** both games hold 60 FPS with no frame over 25 ms. Memory grows by 24 MB in Godot and 51 MB on macOS, so nothing leaks. The node count rises by 1,006, which is exactly 503 trail segments (each shows up as two Godot nodes); that matches the macOS trail code and stops at the per-racer cap. The texture churn the earlier report saw only happens on sand: about 49 textures per second in the dunes, none in the town after the first minute.

**Loading:** the loading screen freezes for 2.8–3.4 s at 93%, against 0.75 s on macOS. Of that, 2.6 s is the SceneKit-compatibility layer handing all 4,884 nodes to Godot at once (SceneKit does this work in the background), and 0.3 s is encoding a screenshot to PNG that is then thrown away. Launch to race takes 13.1 s against 8.6 s.

**Transitions:** the "2–15 fps transitions" in the earlier report come from the playthrough test's own window captures, which take 260–420 ms each. In actual gameplay the worst transition frames are 19–73 ms.

- `tools/perf`: the window, Metal-label and main-thread-stall libraries, the benchmark runner, and the trace and CPU analysis scripts.

- `tools/sync-assets.py` now keeps the `.wav` files raw, so an export plays the same audio as the editor run. It previously exported without race audio.
- The Godot 4.7.2 .NET export templates are now installed.

===== GPU
I reduced Godot's GPU work per 1080p frame by about 3 ms in the race and 1.4 ms in the town roam. The camera image did not change. Most of the remaining gap to macOS sits inside Godot's renderer, which the game cannot change. All four commits are in the worktree. I could not confirm that the hook pushed them.

**Kept (2 changes):**
- **SSAO depth mips:** the SSAO port now keeps its depth mip chain in a one-channel texture. Before, it mip-mapped all four channels of a half-float RGBA texture, although only the depth is read past the first level. The output is bit-identical. The SSAO step drops from 2.6 ms to 1.8–1.9 ms per frame in a fixed 1080p town view. A faster single-pass version was tried first and dropped because it was not bit-exact.
- **Simplified robot meshes for shadows only:** the robots' CAD meshes (Marvin alone is 695,000 triangles) now cast shadows from Godot's own simplified versions. The camera and the depth pre-pass still draw the full mesh. Each simplified version is used only while it is within half a pixel of the full mesh. Shadow maps drop from about 2.6 ms to 1.6–2.2 ms, and robot shadows change by at most 0.003/255. An option (off) also lets the camera use the simplified meshes. It saves another 0.5–1 ms, but robot outlines then move slightly, so I left it off.

**Results at 1920x1080, 45-second benchmark, two runs each:**

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Race FPS | 32.8 | 36.4 |
| Race GPU work per frame | 23.9 ms | 20.9 ms |
| Town roam FPS | 29.1 | 29.7 |
| Town roam GPU work per frame | 24.1 ms | 22.7 ms |

The town roam's frame rate barely moves because the GPU is shared: a MarvinSimulator left running and the window server use 270–350 GPU-ms per second in every run. At 960x540 both builds hold 60 FPS. macOS needs 11.0 ms per frame at 1080p.

**Tried and dropped, all measured:**
- 8 shadow-filter samples instead of 16 (SceneKit's count): no gain. Godot's soft filter costs about 4 ms over the hard filter whatever the sample count.
- A shared-memory SSAO blur, testing the shadow box once per pixel instead of per light, skipping fully transparent overlay pixels, and a cheaper sky-light lookup: no gains beyond the run-to-run noise.

**Where the rest goes:**
- **Composed shading:** the lighting function costs 1.6 ms and the sky lookups 0.7 ms, but only if removed whole.
- **Robot draw calls:** about 760 per frame. Each robot part is its own draw with its own material.
- **Ground overlays:** trampled sand 1.7 ms, streets 1.2 ms.

MEAS: Setup: Mac mini M2, 1x display, Godot editor runtime (Debug C#, compiled optimised), `--town-benchmark` at daylight 0.5, window exactly 1920x1080 or 960x540. Each run waited until no other Godot or Marvin process was running, but other agents' jobs shared the machine all day. The user's MarvinSimulator and WindowServer used 270–350 GPU-ms per second in every run. The same build varies by about ±0.7 ms per frame between runs, so totals come from interleaved repeats.

**45-second benchmark, moving camera, 1920x1080, two runs per build** (FPS from benchmark.json; GPU work per frame from a labelled Metal System Trace at 20–24 s; walltime from metalperftrace):

All 17 commits from the three optimisation branches are now on codex/mos-aster-racing-city in the main checkout. I applied them one at a time in the order GPU, CPU, release. Two files were changed by both the GPU and CPU branches and had to be merged by hand, keeping both changes:

**Why 1080p is still at about 30:** Godot needs about 21–23 ms of graphics work per frame where SceneKit needs 11 ms. Most of the remaining gap is inside Godot's own renderer, which the game code can't reach:
- Its soft-shadow filter costs about 4 ms more than hard shadows, whatever the sample count.
- It clears the whole 8192² shadow map every frame.
- Its terrain and transparent ground layers cost about 3 ms more than SceneKit's.

**Options, all your call:**

content.text:
Option 2 is in and pushed, and it costs more look than I said it would. At 1920×1080 the town now runs at 40 FPS (was 30) and the race at 47 FPS (was 35). Close to the camera the hard shadows are clearly blocky.

**What changed:**
- **Shadows:** the game now uses hard shadows by default. The exact SceneKit look stays available with `MARVIN_SCN_CAL=Exact`, which renders pixel for pixel like the previous build.
- **Robot meshes:** the camera now uses the simplified robot meshes too.
- **Commits:** 5 in total. Four implement and document the change. The fifth is a second agent's correction of three wrong statements in the docs.

**Checked by the second agent:**
- It re-measured the gain and it holds.
- No new shadow acne or light leaks.
- The core checks are still byte-identical to Swift, and every test mode passes except the two random-grid or Mac-failing ones from before.

**The close-up problem:** in the image above (Mac | previous soft shadows | hard shadows), Marvin's head throws a stair-stepped band across his body and the ground shadow is saw-toothed. That view is framed like the race chase camera, so players see this all the time. Other changes:
- robot close-ups and dune contacts show big shadow blocks;
- shadows from the two suns show double, jagged edges;
- the faint menu and sandbox shadows now have sharp outlines.

The average difference from macOS across all captures went from 1.79 to 1.97/255.

**Now running:** a fix for the blockiness that keeps the speed (at most +0.5 ms of graphics work at 1080p):
- **Finer near-camera shadows:** shrink the first shadow-map split to cover only the near range, so that region gets much finer texels. This uses the existing maps, so it should cost almost nothing.
- **Motion check:** look for shadow crawl while the camera moves, which hasn't been tested yet.
- **Independent check:** a second agent re-measures and compares crops of Mac, soft, previous hard and new hard shadows.

**Housekeeping:**
- **Disk space:** Instruments trace files had filled the disk twice. The agents deleted only those leftover traces, and the benchmark script now cleans up after itself.

result.output:
I checked 233da48 against the commit before it (38818a3), built from its own tree. The report is right about the town roam and about MARVIN_SCN_CAL=Exact. It is wrong about the race speed-up, and it overstates "the blocks are gone". I corrected the docs in one commit (4ebf6c0), with its own Entire checkpoint, and pushed it.

**1. Scope.** 233da48 is the only commit after 38818a3. It changes:
- **Shadow fit (SceneKitRuntime.cs):** with the hard filter, each fixed-box sun now gets four splits ending at 12, 30 and 58 m. The last split ends at the box's farthest point in view, rounded up to 58 × 1.25^k. The normal-bias scale is adjusted for the smaller splits.
- **Settings (SceneKitCalibration.cs):** new HardShadowSplit*/FarStep settings, and BaseTerrainCastsShadow=false. Exact switches the terrain's shadow back on.
- **DirtWorld.cs:** the base terrain casts only when that setting is on.
- **GroundBiasProbe.cs:** a new test E (a thin plate seen through the race camera's lens).
- **New ShadowMotionProbe.cs:** adds `--shadow-motion-probe`.
- **Docs:** PORTING.md and docs/performance.md.

Nothing in apps/simulator-macos or tools/ changed. I checked the terrain claim against the geometry. The base terrain is a flat 256 m square at y=-0.025, and the desert around it never goes below -0.025, so its shadow cannot land on anything visible.

**2. Speed.** Town roam reproduces: +1.1 FPS, 0.58 ms less GPU time per frame. The moving race does not: four interleaved rounds give 53.4 FPS before and 52.5 after, within the runs' spread. So the race is about as fast as before, not 1 FPS faster. The frozen race-start and town frames do get faster (0.46 and 0.39 ms).

**3. Look (by eye, one capture per configuration).** The previous build's large blurred blocks are gone, and mid-range shadows are cleaner:
- Marvin's head shadow crosses its body as a clean line (track-closeup-3).
- The table and pane shadows in race_midday_chase have straight edges.

In the closest views the texels still show, now as small crisp stair-steps:
- 4–12 px steps: walle-gear, marvin-gear, r2d2-wheels, WALL-E-contact.
- 1–3 px steps: walking-480 feet, the base of the household-2 wall, the ground shadow in track-closeup-11.

So blockiness is reduced, not gone. One artefact is worse: the dome in front of the camera in shadow-angle-15 shows blotchy dark patches on itself, which macOS does not show. menu_portrait and sandbox are unchanged. Every shadow-related capture moved further from macOS (closeups-race 2.005→2.235/255, dune-contact 2.67→3.00, visual-regression 1.09→1.20).

**4. Motion.** In a 30 s race driven at fixed 1/60 s steps with the chase camera, the last split changed size in 44 frames (sun A) and 37 (sun B). The old fit changed it in nearly every frame. The new rounding has no hysteresis, so near a step the size can flip back and forth (sun B 72.5→58→72.5 m within four frames). At driving speed those frames change no more shadow pixels than their neighbours. The committed probe reproduces the reported stability numbers. I saw no split seams in the frames I looked at.

**5. Exact mode** is pixel-identical to 38818a3 in calibration, closeups, closeups-race, menu and visual-regression. Where images differ (smoke, dune-contact, entrance, people), the same files differ by the same amounts between two runs of 38818a3 alone. Reports are identical apart from one timing field (cpuUpdateP95MS).

**6. Trailers and origin.** 233da48 has the Co-Authored-By, Claude-Session and Entire-Checkpoint trailers, and its checkpoint (01M47DM7TMPN6AH4JENEA7HC5Z) is on origin. My commit and its checkpoint are pushed, and origin matches HEAD.

**Doc fix (4ebf6c0).** It adds the measurements against 38818a3 and says the race is about as fast as before. It says close views keep small crisp stair-steps, describes the dome patches correctly, and records the driving check.

The side-by-side image (macOS | soft exact | previous hard | new hard) is at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-m1/071026d1-7915-4c92-80a5-434d94756a72/scratchpad/hard-shadow-before-after.png. Working files are in scratchpad/verify. I deleted my own build copies and motion frames; 106 GB are free.
MEAS: 1920x1080, editor runtime, M2. Before = 38818a3 built from its own tree; after = 233da48. Same runner, `--wait-idle`, interleaved before/after/after/before. No other game process was running and the MarvinSimulator was not running. GPU walltime is from metalperftrace.

| race, 45 s, 4 rounds | 53.13, 53.96, 54.08, 52.29 FPS (mean 53.4); 18.98, 18.66, 18.73, 19.42 ms (18.95) | 53.06, 51.76, 53.58, 51.77 FPS (mean 52.5); 18.96, 19.49, 18.90, 19.57 ms (19.23) | −0.8 FPS, +0.28 ms, within each build's 1.8 FPS spread (claimed gain not reproduced) |

**Better:**
- **track-closeup-3:** the previous wavy, stair-stepped head shadow on Marvin's body is now one clean line. A small step remains on the ground at the left.
- **race_midday_chase:** the table and pane shadows went from saw-tooth to straight edges. Each now has the weaker sun's lighter band beside it, with a crisp edge.

content.text:
I've started the shadow setting and the next performance round. In Fast mode at 1920×1080, Godot needs about 22 ms per frame in the town, and 60 FPS means getting under 16.7 ms.

**Shadow setting:** "Shadow quality: Exact / Fast" goes on the Settings screen, saved with your other settings, defaulting to Fast. The Mac Settings screen has no such option, so it'll be documented as an intended difference. `MARVIN_SCN_CAL` still overrides it for tests.

**What's next for 60 FPS**, three levers:

1. **Optimisations that don't change the look (started now, three parallel tracks):**
   - **Ground:** the town ground's procedural noise costs about 2.2 ms per frame, and about 15 stacked transparent ground layers cost about 3 ms. The noise never changes, so it can be computed once into textures at load, and layers that share a material can be merged.
   - **Shading and post-processing:** the lighting function (about 1.6 ms), sky lookups (0.7), depth pre-pass (1.0), glow (1.0) and anti-aliasing resolves (0.7) all have room to get cheaper.
   - **Draw calls:** the robots alone take about 760 per frame; merging parts that move together would cut that.

   Each change is kept only if it's measurably faster and the screenshots stay identical. If most of this pans out, Fast mode should get to about 60 FPS in the race and close to it in the town. Exact mode would stay in the 40s, because Godot's soft shadow filter alone costs about 4 ms.

2. **Render below 1080p and upscale:** Godot 4.7 supports Apple's MetalFX on the Mac and AMD's FSR 2 everywhere. Rendering 3D at about 75% and upscaling to 1080p would very likely give 60 FPS in both modes. The image gets slightly softer, plus some upscaler artefacts on fine detail. It would be another setting ("Render scale").

3. **Patch Godot itself:** a custom engine build with SceneKit-style soft shadows (an 8-sample filter on fixed per-sun maps, without clearing the whole shadow atlas every frame). 2. **One-pass shadow maps:** all sun shadow maps render in one pass, with no separate full clear. This should give an identical image.
3. **SceneKit-style soft filter:** a fixed kernel of taps, with no per-pixel noise. One mode loops at runtime, the way SceneKit's own compiled shader does.
4. **Fixed shadow box:** one fixed, world-anchored shadow map per sun (4096 and 2048, as in SceneKit), instead of our split emulation.

All of them are off unless switched on, so stock behaviour stays the default.

**Still unproven:** why Godot's soft filter costs about 4 ms, and therefore whether the new filter gets close to hard-shadow cost. The reviewer found the "8 samples cost the same as 16" evidence weaker than claimed. The build stage will measure it first with Xcode's shader profiler.

- **macOS builds:** universal (Apple Silicon and Intel), Metal only.
- **One-pass maps (patch 2):** on at every Graphics Detail level, as long as the captures are byte-identical.
- **SceneKit's shadow sample offsets:** I'll measure them from a Metal frame capture of SceneKit. The earlier dump of SceneKit's shader source was in a temporary folder and is gone, but the README quotes the relevant code.

All three look-preserving optimisation tracks are done, and the integration step is merging them. Nine commits are already on `codex/mos-aster-racing-city`, each with its own Entire checkpoint and pushed. It's now running the before/after look comparison (ground-performance captures at the moment) and will then measure again.

**What each track gained** (1920×1080, each measured against the same starting build):

| Track | Fast, town | Fast, race | Exact, town | Exact, race |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shading (light loops, sky lookup, unused shader paths) | 46 → 52 FPS | 52 → 57 | 35 → 38 | 40 → 48 |
| Ground (noise from a precomputed table, skipping known results) | 46 → 49 | 52 → 53 | 34.5 → 35.7 | no gain |
| Draw calls (halved by instancing) | no change | no change | no change | no change |

The ground change keeps town captures pixel-identical. The combined result comes from the integration step's final measurement. Adding the shading and ground gains, I'd expect Fast to land around 53–55 FPS in the town and about 57 in the race, so not yet 60.

**Biggest remaining cost:** the stacked transparent ground layers in town. The trampled-sand layer alone costs about 3.5 ms per frame, the streets about 1.8 ms.

**Next:** when integration finishes, I'll build the Graphics Detail setting (Max / High / Medium / Low). Upscaling at High and below is what gets the game to 60 FPS.

Both checks are done. The implementing agent hasn't finished its docs yet, so I'm waiting for it before stopping the workflow; a background watcher will tell me when it returns. Its README, PORTING.md and performance-doc changes aren't committed yet.

**Windows upscaler path:** it looks correct on inspection. Nothing in it assumes Metal.
- On Direct3D 12 and Vulkan, Medium and Low use FSR 2, because MetalFX isn't available there.
- Without Godot's main renderer, they fall back to plain bilinear scaling.
- Anti-aliasing is switched off whenever a temporal upscaler is on.

It hasn't been run on Windows.

**Look review** (the race-start sheet above, crops at 2×, plus a motion frame from Medium):
- **High:** close to Max. The visible difference is that removing ambient occlusion lightens contact areas a little, such as under the robots and around R2-D2's dome. Distant signs and the crowd are essentially unchanged.
- **Medium and Low:** noticeably softer than Max, with jagged edges on robot outlines and thin seams. Distant sign text ("GATES 1-2") becomes unreadable, and the brick wall looks pixelated. Low is a bit worse than Medium.
- **Motion:** in the driving frame at Medium I saw no ghost trails behind Marvin, only the same jagged edges. The HUD stays sharp at all levels because it's drawn at full resolution.
- **Edge quality at Medium and Low:** the edges are more jagged than a temporal upscaler normally gives. That suggests it isn't reconstructing edges well. I haven't confirmed the cause.

Once the implementing agent commits its docs, I'll stop the workflow so the separate verification never runs, then report back.

## Graphics detail: four levels, Max as before
Measured on 2026-10-06 on the same Mac (M2, nothing else on the GPU: `run-benchmark.py --wait-idle`, no other game
process in any run). The Settings screen has a Graphics detail row next to Shadow quality (Godot-only; PORTING.md, "Known
deviations"): **Max**, the default, is the renderer as it was; **High**, **Medium** and **Low** trade look for GPU time.
The two settings are independent: no level touches the shadows. Game modes, the benchmarks included, keep Max unless
`MARVIN_GRAPHICS_DETAIL` selects a level, as Shadow quality keeps Fast unless `MARVIN_SCN_CAL` says otherwise.
| level | what it changes (each level contains the one above it) |
|---|---|
| Max | nothing: full resolution, 2x MSAA in the race world (4x in the sandbox and menu), SceneKit's SSAO, every effect as before |
| High | full resolution; no SSAO (`SsaoEnabled`: the robots and the track walls lose their ambient occlusion, the town has almost none of it in SceneKit either, because its `.geometry`-modified materials receive none); mesh LODs for the robots' small parts (`MeshLodMinTriangles` 256: track shoes and ribs, wheels, within half a pixel); one bilinear tap per glow level instead of bicubic (`GlowBicubicUpscale`); the sky reflection of everything but the robots from the sky light's spherical harmonics instead of the pre-filtered radiance bands (`SimpleSkyReflection`); 2x instead of 4x anisotropic filtering |
| Medium | the 3D view at 0.6 of the drawable's width and height, upscaled by MetalFX temporal (FSR 2 on Windows), which replaces MSAA; the ground's overlay layers (trampled sand, streets, doorway patches, aprons) lit with diffuse light only (`SimpleGroundLighting`: no direct specular, the sky reflection from the spherical harmonics) |
| Low | the 3D view at half the drawable's width and height; no anisotropic filtering; SceneKit's levels of detail (buildings, crowd, dune tiles) switching at 0.6 of their distances (`LodDistanceScale`); the robots' mesh LODs at up to 2 pixels of error instead of half a pixel (`MeshLodThreshold`) |
The HUD, menus and loading screen are AppKit views drawn over the 3D view's texture, at full resolution at every level.
### What Godot 4.7.2 offers
From its source (`servers/rendering/renderer_viewport.cpp`, `render_forward_clustered.cpp`, the Metal driver) and on
this Mac: `Viewport.scaling_3d_mode` bilinear, nearest, FSR 1 (spatial), FSR 2.2 (temporal; Forward+ on every
RenderingDevice driver: Metal, Direct3D 12, Vulkan), MetalFX spatial and MetalFX temporal (Metal driver only, when the
device supports them; this M2 supports both, MetalFX temporal for input scales 0.333 to 1). Under MetalFX temporal Godot
turns 3D MSAA off itself (with a warning); FSR 2 and MetalFX temporal replace TAA; both accumulate frames jittered over
8 / scale^2 phases with a texture mipmap bias of log2(scale); their motion vectors are the depth buffer reprojected by the
camera's motion plus a motion pass that draws the instances whose transform changed (the crowd's walk, which a
`.geometry` modifier animates, and the particles have no motion vectors of their own). Godot upscales after the
transparent pass, so glow and tone mapping run at the drawable's size. Where MetalFX temporal is unavailable (an older
GPU, or a scale outside its limits) Godot would fall back to MetalFX spatial or FSR 2 with a warning; the facade chooses
itself (`SCNView.Upscalers`): MetalFX temporal, else FSR 2, else bilinear (no RenderingDevice, the Compatibility
renderer), and turns MSAA off for both temporal upscalers. FSR 2 on Direct3D 12 and Vulkan was not run (no Windows
machine); on Metal it is selectable for measurements (`RenderUpscaler=4`).

at the race start, dust and dirt), 28 s runs, a labelled trace 21-25 s after the start. GPU walltime per frame is

`race-start-exact.png`, and from the capture modes at 1280 x 820, `capture-r2d2-wheels.png` (the smoke test's race-track close-up), `capture-dirt-grid.png`, `capture-household-5.png` (the pinned entrance test) and `capture-sandbox.png` (whose course rings are random); gitignored like the other comparison sheets):
| frozen frame | High | Medium | Low |
|---|---|---|---|
| town view, Fast | 0.33/255, 0.5 % | 3.12/255, 4.9 % | 3.24/255, 6.4 % |
| town view, Exact | 0.32/255, 0.5 % | 3.09/255, 4.8 % | 3.19/255, 6.2 % |
| race start, Fast | 1.70/255, 6.4 % | 2.84/255, 10.0 % | 3.15/255, 11.4 % |
| race start, Exact | 1.70/255, 6.6 % | 2.85/255, 10.1 % | 3.01/255, 10.5 % |
(Exact against Fast at Max: 0.38/255 in the town view and 1.47/255 at the race start, the soft shadow edges.)
What changes, from the sheets and the capture modes run at each level (`--menu-smoke-test`, `--smoke-test` and `--town-smoke-test` with
their pins, `--visual-regression-test`, the pinned `--entrance-smoke-test` and `--dune-contact-test`, each with
`MARVIN_GRAPHICS_DETAIL` set, all passing; mean |difference| from Max over the captures, High / Medium / Low: smoke
0.70 / 1.96 / 2.26 (two Max runs 0.10), town 0.36 / 3.06 / 3.35 (0.05), entrance 0.11 / 2.67 / 2.90, menu 0.01 / 0.46 /
0.65; the visual regression and dune contact tests capture through an `SCNRenderer`, which keeps full resolution, so
only their SSAO and small changes show, 0.6 and 1.2/255 at every level):
- **High**: the robots and the ground around them lose SceneKit's ambient occlusion: Marvin's head no longer darkens
  its body and the sand under it in the town view (3.1/255 in that crop), R2-D2's dome and Marvin's head are 5.3-5.7/255
  lighter at the race start, the track around the robots and in their tread ruts up to 8/255 (the town's buildings and
  ground keep their look, 0.03-0.3/255, because SceneKit gives their `.geometry`-modified materials no SSAO). The other
  four changes stay within the two Max runs' difference: the robots' small parts (track shoes, ribs, wheels) drawn from
  levels within half a pixel, the glow around highlights by up to a few levels, the rough surfaces' faint sky reflection
  from the spherical harmonics, the sand's texture at grazing angles a little softer with 2x anisotropy. Edges, text and
  textures are as sharp as at Max.
- **Medium**: the 3D view is drawn at 1152 x 648 and MetalFX upscales it: fine detail softens (the sand's ripples and
  tread marks, the signs' small text, which becomes hard to read at a distance: "GATES 1-2" at the race start), edges
  are anti-aliased by the upscaler instead of MSAA (smooth at rest, the hard shadows' stair-steps a little coarser), and
  the ground's overlay layers lose their direct specular: the sand about 1 % darker (most of the town view's 3.1/255).
  In motion (the playthrough's live window captures at Medium and Low, racing and orbiting the camera) the moving
  robots and the track show no trails and the image stays as soft as at rest; the crowd's walk and the dust, which have
  no motion vectors of their own, were not examined frame by frame.
- **Low**: 960 x 540 upscaled: everything softer again (the robots' panel lines, R2-D2's dome details), the ground's
  textures without anisotropic filtering blur towards the horizon, the crowd and the town's buildings switch to their
  coarser levels closer (at 0.6 of SceneKit's distances), the robots' silhouettes may move by up to 2 pixels.
### Switching, loading and hitches
The level **applies live**: activating the row stores the choice and calls `GraphicsDetailSetting.apply`, which sets
the fields and `SceneKitRuntime.GraphicsDetailChanged`: every view's render scale, upscaler, MSAA, anisotropy and mesh
LOD threshold at once, the glow filter at once, the robots' small-part meshes once their levels are prepared on worker
threads (they draw their old meshes until then), the composer's variants and SceneKit's LOD distances when a scene is next
drawn (`ObserveShading`) or prepared (`PrepareAsync`: a race world cached from an earlier race rebuilds behind the loading
screen, spread over frames). The row is only on the Settings screen, so no race or sandbox frame waits for a switch, but
the switch itself is not free: the frame after the click (menu check, frame times printed per switch, three runs) took
95-106 ms to High (SSAO off: the prepass without the normal-roughness buffer; the anisotropy; the robots' meshes), 150-290
ms to Medium and 155-172 ms to Low (Godot rebuilds the view's render buffers and MetalFX creates its scaler for the new
input size) and 37-45 ms back to Max; every later frame took 16.7 ms. Once, on the first switch to Medium after the build
had been exported, the switch took 0.63 s and the next frame 1.01 s, with one "timeout waiting for fence" from Godot's
Metal driver (the GPU was still busy with MetalFX's first use); later runs did not repeat it. Before a view could be freed
with MetalFX temporal configured but never drawn (the menu check's second settings view), every later frame timed out
on a fence (1 s per frame); views outside the scene tree now get no upscaler (`SCNView.ApplyRenderScaling`), and the
menu check passes without a timeout. The first run of a new configuration after a build also compiles pipelines while
it draws (main-thread stalls of 50-400 ms over the first seconds in the frozen-view runs); the benchmarks below ran a
short warm-up of every level and configuration first. Loading (`--loading-smoke-test` under the runner): Max and Medium
both pass in 11.5 and 11.8 s with 458 and 463 responsive ticks and the same stalls (the longest, 1.8 and 2.0 s, at
launch); a first run at Medium right after other configurations had run spent 41 s in main-thread stalls, 27 s of them at
the race's reveal, compiling pipelines, and its repeat did not. At the reveal, the snapshot `revealDirtTrack` takes (and
discards) draws the race view once per jitter phase under the temporal upscaler (23 draws at Medium, 32 at Low), which
the loading screen covers.
